title: Citation integrity: Concern did not determine appeal
desc: Identifies suspicious citations without proving AI fabrication, while grounding the documented result in ordinary procedural and evidential deficiencies.

kps.k: The extracts raise a serious citation-integrity concern but do not establish an AI hallucination incident or the later strike-out ruling.
kps.d: In Bandla v SRA, the judge flagged concerns about authorities in maintained appeal grounds, while recording that the SRA’s solicitors assembled 53 cited cases that existed. The judge expressly separated that issue from the extension-of-time decision. Despite the source’s headline, the supplied extracts neither establish that AI generated the problematic citations nor provide findings about 25 non-existent authorities or the later abuse-of-process reasoning. Their contribution to the legal-AI debate therefore concerns citation reliability, not demonstrated AI causation or a measured model error rate.

qs.q: As to cases “which exist”, there is in this case a specific and very serious concern about caselaw which the Appellant cited to the court in grounds of appeal which he has maintained.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: The SRA’s solicitors have, as I have explained, also prepared a bundle containing the 53 cases cited by the Appellant which exist.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The documented outcome rests on ordinary procedural and evidential grounds independent of the citation concern.
kps.d: The court refused permission to appeal late after a delay of seven years, two months and 26 days. It found that sending the SDT’s reasons in June 2017 started the appeal period and rejected Bandla’s demand for personal service under the Hague Convention. Contradictory accounts undermined his denial of receipt. The practical distinction matters: the extracts support a refusal to extend time, not a conclusion that defective citations caused that refusal.

qs.q: It has reliably been calculated by the SRA as 7 years 2 months and 26 days.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: For all these reasons, I find that the statement of reasons were “sent” as claimed by the SRA and time for the appeal therefore began in June 2017.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The court distinguished evidence of illness and efforts to obtain representation from evidence sufficient to excuse the delay.
kps.d: Bandla attributed years of delay to schizophrenia and the subsequent period to difficulty securing affordable representation. The judge acknowledged evidence of mental ill-health and corroborated contacts with prospective lawyers in 2024, but found no adequate evidence that illness prevented an appeal throughout the relevant years; clinical records described stability in 2022–23. The court separately found no present capacity issue. It balanced access to appeal against regulatory finality, public protection and confidence, concluding that refusal did not impair the essence of the Article 6 appeal right. The case illustrates the importance of evidence connecting a claimed impediment to the relevant period, rather than treating diagnosis or representation difficulties as automatically decisive.

qs.q: Applying the guidance of Underhill LJ from J v K, it is very clear that the sort of evidence needed, covering the relevant periods of time, so as to explain or excuse the failure to institute an appeal, is absent in this case.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: They include that on 12 October 2022 the Appellant’s mental health condition was “very well controlled”; that on 17 October 2022 it was “stable”; that on 29 March 2023 he was “mentally stable”; and that again on 26 July 2023 he was “mentally stable”.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The underlying appeal’s evidential weakness also informed the refusal; procedural objections did not displace the documented regulatory case.
kps.d: The judge found that delivery of disciplinary documents satisfied the applicable rules and that the SDT had considered available mental-health material before proceeding in Bandla’s absence. On substance, the court contrasted evidence of firm abandonment and misleading insurance information with his unsupported allegation of broker fraud. It assessed both the procedural challenge and the challenge to the findings and sanction as weak. These findings concern the merits of this proposed appeal, not a general rule that citation defects negate otherwise valid legal arguments.

qs.q: It was plainly sufficient, to comply with those rules, that the relevant documents were taken to and left at the relevant address.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: I am unable to accept that there is anything approaching a strong case, as the Appellant claims, based on any procedural impropriety on the part of the SDT.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The court source supports the cluster’s principal proposition. It identifies a serious citation-integrity concern but expressly separates that concern from the extension-of-time decision; the supplied material also does not establish that AI caused any defective citations. The documented refusal instead rests on conventional procedural and evidential grounds, especially the delay of more than seven years, valid sending of the judgment, unreliable evidence about receipt, insufficient medical evidence covering the relevant period, and weak proposed appeal grounds. The main internal variation is therefore one of emphasis rather than position: the court regarded citation integrity as potentially serious, while declining to let that unresolved issue affect this particular decision. As this facet contains one curated court source, it demonstrates this source’s reasoning rather than a general position shared by regulators, courts and professional bodies.

qs.q: It has reliably been calculated by the SRA as 7 years 2 months and 26 days.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: For now, I put that matter entirely to one side.
qs.a: Bandla v Solicitors Regulation Authority — High Court Strikes Out Appeal Grounds on Its Own Motion as Abuse of Process for Citation of 25 Non-Existent Authorities · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the cluster’s principal proposition. It identifies a serious concern about cited authorities but shows that the court expressly put that issue aside when deciding the extension application. The documented refusal instead rested on conventional procedural and evidential grounds, especially the delay of more than seven years, the finding that time began in June 2017, unreliable evidence about receipt, inadequate medical evidence covering the relevant period, and weak proposed appeal grounds. Material internal variation lies between the source’s expansive headline and the narrower supplied extracts: the extracts flag citation-integrity concerns, but do not establish AI fabrication, findings concerning 25 non-existent authorities, or the later abuse-of-process ruling. Because the curated evidence contains only this source for the period, it supports the proposition in this instance but cannot establish how prevalent this treatment was across 2025 sources generally.
